summary: Specifies the Point-to-Point Protocol, a way to carry multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links, as a Draft Standard. When it became a full standard it would be recommended for all TCP/IP implementations on serial links. It was replaced by RFC 1331.

plainLanguage.summary: If two computers share one wire, they need rules for packing messages. This is the rule book for that.

questions: point to point protocol draft standard
how does ppp establish a connection
subtitle: How to send multiple protocols over a single point-to-point serial link.

tldr.problem: Two computers connected by a serial link need standard rules for sending messages with different protocols, and a way to configure the connection automatically.
tldr.mechanism: PPP defines a frame format for encapsulating datagrams, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) to set up and maintain the connection, and Network Control Protocols (NCP) to negotiate individual network-layer protocols like IP.
tldr.outcome: PPP became the standard for dialup and serial connections. It was later updated and became RFC 1331 as a full standard, and RFC 1661 modernized it further.

today: RFC 1171 was replaced by RFC 1331 as a full Internet Standard, and then RFC 1661 modernized the protocol further. However, PPP remains the fundamental standard for point-to-point serial links and continues to be used in dialup connections, PPPoE (over Ethernet), and other serial protocols.

sections.title: What PPP Does
sections.content:
PPP—the Point-to-Point Protocol—solves a fundamental problem: two computers connected by a serial link need a standard way to exchange data from multiple network protocols (like IP, DECnet, or AppleTalk) over the same wire.

PPP has three key pieces: a way to frame and encapsulate data, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) to establish and configure the connection, and Network Control Protocols (NCP) to set up individual network-layer protocols. This lets systems negotiate capabilities automatically instead of requiring manual configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP is the agreement for how to send messages across a serial cable. It handles not just one kind of data, but lets you pick and choose what you need.

sections.title: Frame Format and Encapsulation
sections.content:
Every PPP frame follows a standard structure: a flag byte (01111110) marks the start, followed by an address field (always 0xff for all-stations), a control field (0x03 for unnumbered information), a 16-bit protocol field, the data payload, a 16-bit frame check sequence (FCS) for error detection, and a closing flag.

The protocol field identifies what kind of data is inside: values starting with c (like 0xc021) are for LCP control messages; values starting with 8 (like 0x8021 for IP Control Protocol) are for network protocol negotiation; values starting with 0 (like 0x0021 for IP itself) are for actual data. This design lets PPP multiplex different protocols over a single link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is wrapped in a standard envelope: a flag at the start, a label saying what kind of message it is, the message itself, a checksum, and a flag at the end.

sections.title: Link Establishment and the LCP State Machine
sections.content:
Before any data can flow, PPP goes through four phases. Phase 1 (Link Establishment) uses LCP to exchange Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak and Configure-Reject packets until both sides agree on parameters. Phase 2 (Link Quality Determination) is optional; it tests the link quality using Echo-Request and Echo-Reply packets. Phase 3 (Network-Layer Protocol Negotiation) uses Network Control Protocols to configure protocols like IP. Phase 4 (Link Termination) closes the connection with Terminate-Request and Terminate-Ack packets.

LCP uses a finite-state machine with seven states: Closed (initial), Listen (waiting for peer), Req-Sent (waiting for acknowledgment), Ack-Rcvd (received ack but not sent one), Ack-Sent (sent ack but not received one), Open (both sides agreed), and Closing (terminating). A Restart timer (default 3 seconds) retransmits requests if the peer does not respond; after ten retransmissions the link closes.
sections.plainLanguage: Bringing up a link is like a handshake: you ask your peer if they agree to certain settings, they say yes or no, you both confirm, you test the connection, then you can use it. If someone doesn't answer, you ask again. If they still don't answer, you give up.

sections.title: Configuration Options and Network Protocols
sections.content:
LCP allows both sides to negotiate optional features and capabilities through Configuration Options. Each option has a type (identifying the capability), a length, and a data field. Options can be accepted (Configure-Ack), negotiated (Configure-Nak, suggesting a different value), or refused (Configure-Reject, meaning the option is not understood).

Once LCP reaches the Open state, Network Control Protocols (NCP) take over to configure individual network-layer protocols. The Internet Protocol Control Protocol (IPCP) is the most common; it uses the same Configure/Ack/Nak/Reject packet types as LCP, but operates only after LCP is open. Only once both LCP and IPCP are open can actual IP datagrams flow across the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Configuration is a back-and-forth negotiation. One side says 'I want feature X', the other says 'yes' or 'how about Y instead', and they keep going until they agree or give up.

sections.title: Link Maintenance and Debugging
sections.content:
PPP includes several maintenance and debugging facilities for use when the link is open. Echo-Request and Echo-Reply packets provide a loopback mechanism to test both directions of the link. Discard-Request packets let one side test the local-to-remote direction by sending data that the peer simply discards. Code-Reject packets report unknown LCP message types, and Protocol-Reject packets notify the peer that an unsupported protocol was received.

These facilities help detect link problems, measure performance, and debug connectivity issues without disrupting the data path.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the link is running, you can ping it to make sure both directions work, send junk data as a stress test, and report errors if something breaks.
